name: Pediatric medial approach to the distal femur
corridor: Posterior border of vastus medialis with optional proximal extension between vastus medialis and adductor magnus

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the knee flexed to relax medial tissues and permit posterior sartorial retraction.

setup.text: Identify the tension-side reduction block on imaging, map the physis and vascular status, and have vascular support available when arterial injury is suspected.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark medial joint line, adductor tubercle, posterior vastus-medialis border, patella, physis, and metaphyseal fragment.

incision.text: Use a 4-5 cm straight incision from the joint line proximally along the posterior vastus-medialis border, extending as needed.

superficial_interval.text: Identify, incise, and mobilize the distal posterior edge of vastus medialis while protecting medial sensory and venous structures.

deep_interval.text: Retract vastus medialis anteriorly to expose physis and metaphysis; for proximal/posterior extension retract sartorius and adductor magnus posteriorly while remaining on bone.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, vastus-medialis fascia, medial muscle interval, periosteum and physis, with optional posterior adductor plane.

structures_encountered.text: Vastus medialis, entrapped periosteum, physis, distal metaphysis, sartorius, adductor-magnus tendon, capsule, and popliteal space may be encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Popliteal artery and vein, tibial nerve, saphenous structures, medial genicular vessels, physis, periosteal blood supply, and cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The popliteal bundle lies immediately posterior to the femur; all posterior extension must be blunt, controlled, and kept on bone.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid forceful posterior retraction, epiphyseal stripping, or repeated reduction across the high-risk distal-femoral physis.

exposure.text: Exposes medial physis and metaphysis directly, with extensions for medial articular lesions, limited posterior access, or vascular exploration.

limitations.text: Posterior articular visualization remains limited and broad anterior articular reconstruction may require a parapatellar approach.

extensions.text: Extend proximally to sartorius and adductor magnus, bluntly develop posterior access, or add a capsulotomy for selected joint inspection.

indications.text: Use after failed closed reduction of medial Salter-Harris II fractures and for medial Hoffa, osteochondral, tumor, or vascular-associated lesions.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose another approach when broad anterior or direct posterior visualization is required or medial soft tissue is compromised.

implant_implications.text: Remove entrapped periosteum, restore physeal anatomy, and use stable fixation with minimal additional physeal or posterior neurovascular risk.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm physeal and articular alignment, medial implant position, and guarded screw length on orthogonal and oblique views.

closure.text: Repair capsulotomy or fascia as used, allow vastus medialis to return anatomically, obtain hemostasis, and close in layers.

complications.text: Complications include popliteal or saphenous injury, growth arrest, deformity, limb-length discrepancy, stiffness, infection, and malreduction.

bailouts.text: Stop blind posterior dissection and add a dedicated exposure or vascular assistance when safe control cannot be achieved.

procedure_applications.condition: A medial Salter-Harris II, medial articular or Hoffa fracture needs direct reduction, or vascular injury requires medial access

questions.question: What commonly blocks Salter-Harris II reduction?
questions.answer: Entrapped periosteum attached to the distal epiphyseal fragment.

questions.question: What is the critical posterior structure?
